critique.good: The Russian terms and Vietnamese translations stay on one line, making the pair easy to scan. Descriptions wrap to two lines, and the equal row heights give the table a steady rhythm.
critique.problems: The first column fits the longest term closely, but the render keeps it intact and legible.
critique.cause: Widths of 173px and 147px give the term and translation columns just enough room for their longest entries, leaving 399px for descriptions.

critique.good: The wider description column gives the explanatory text more breathing room, while the Russian terms remain intact.
critique.problems: Two Vietnamese translations wrap, making the term–translation pairs less immediate to scan. The wider descriptions do not reduce the row heights.
critique.cause: At 105px, the translation column is too narrow for the longer multiword entries; the 441px description column does not yield a compensating reduction in lines.

critique.good: Both term columns are spacious, and all terms and translations stay on one line.
critique.problems: The first description takes three lines, making its row taller and disrupting the otherwise even rhythm. The extra space in the first two columns provides little benefit.
critique.cause: The 205px and 175px term columns leave only 339px for descriptions.

understanding.purpose: A Russian–Vietnamese terminology table pairing technical terms with translations and explanatory descriptions.
understanding.reading: Readers scan the Russian terms, compare each with its Vietnamese equivalent, then read across the row for context. Row height can accommodate naturally wrapped descriptions and, where needed, multiword translations.
groups: Columns 1 and 2 form a term–translation pair; column 3 provides the explanation for that pair.
keep_intact: Individual Russian terms and Vietnamese words, including their diacritics.
The association between each term, translation, and description across its row.
may_wrap: Multiword Vietnamese translations at word boundaries.

bad.why: The Russian terms would have to split within words, while the narrow Vietnamese column would wrap short labels unnecessarily. The extra description width would come at the expense of the two columns readers use to identify each entry.

contrast.why: The Russian terms would have to split within words, while the narrow Vietnamese column would wrap short labels unnecessarily. The extra description width would come at the expense of the two columns readers use to identify each entry.

final.rationale: r0A keeps both the Russian terms and their Vietnamese equivalents on one line, making the pairs easy to scan. It gives the descriptions enough room to sit consistently in two lines, so the rows have an even rhythm. r0B wraps two Vietnamese labels without reducing the table height, while r0C gives the label columns more space than they need and makes the first description three lines tall.

general: Keep paired labels easy to scan together, and give prose enough width to form readable lines.
Judge width changes by their effect on the whole table, including row height and wrapping, rather than by equal column widths or total height alone.
specific: The Russian terms need at least 173px including padding to avoid splitting the longest word.
The Vietnamese labels fit on one line at 147px, leaving most of the available width for descriptions.

final.tradeoffs: r0B gives descriptions more horizontal space, which some readers may prefer, but wraps Vietnamese labels. r0C gives both label columns more breathing room, at the cost of a taller first row.
final.uncertain: The ranges are approximate visual tolerances, not verified breakpoints; the effect of changing one column depends on how the remaining width is redistributed. Designers could reasonably differ on how much extra white space around the labels is worth.

A.why: All three Russian terms break within words, and the Vietnamese header and entries wrap in a cramped column. The description column has ample room, but at too great a cost to the labels.

B.why: Russian terms stay intact and descriptions read comfortably in two lines. The narrower Vietnamese column wraps two entries, making the paired terms less easy to scan.

C.why: Both term columns keep their entries on one line, while descriptions have enough space to read comfortably in two lines. The proportions match the different roles of the columns.

D.why: The equal-looking columns leave large empty areas beside the short terms while the descriptions wrap into three or four lines. This makes the rows tall and weakens comparison across them.

E.why: Both term columns stay on one line, and descriptions remain readable. The extra space given to the term columns leaves the first description on three lines and makes the table less balanced than C.

F.why: Russian terms remain intact and descriptions fit comfortably in two lines. Two Vietnamese entries wrap, making that column harder to scan than in C.

reviews.unsure: B and F appear nearly identical at the displayed scale; any small difference between them is difficult to judge.

A.why: The terms and translations stay intact, but equal column widths leave substantial empty space in the first two columns and force descriptions into three or four lines.

B.why: The narrow first column breaks every Russian term inside a word, and the Vietnamese header and entries also wrap heavily.

C.why: Russian terms remain intact and the descriptions have room to breathe, but two Vietnamese translations wrap onto two lines.

D.why: Both term columns remain on one line, making pairs easy to scan; the narrower description column makes the first description three lines tall.

E.why: Russian terms remain intact and descriptions are readable, though two Vietnamese translations wrap onto two lines.

F.why: Both term columns stay on one line while every description fits in two lines, giving the rows a clear, consistent rhythm.

reviews.unsure: C and E appear nearly identical at this image scale; any small width difference does not visibly change their wrapping.
